XIV A RASH DASH

Nutsy the squirrel was in a great hurry. He always was, especially when the oak trees were showering down their autumn bounty. "More, more, more!" he chattered, his tiny paws a blur as he scooped up acorns. He spotted a particularly large, perfect specimen just at the edge of the creek bank. "That one simply must be mine!" he decided, and with a swift dash, he made for it.

His momentum carried him too far. With a squeak of alarm, Nutsy found himself sliding down the steep, muddy bank. His claws scrabbled uselessly at the slick earth. He landed with a soft splash in the shallow water, his whiskers dripping and his precious acorn, the very one he had so coveted, bobbing away downstream.

Professor Hoot, perched high in a nearby sycamore, observed the scene with a faint click of his beak. "Careful there, young Nutsy!" he hooted, his voice a gentle rumble. "Haste often makes waste, does it not? That acorn, so eagerly pursued, is now quite beyond your grasp."

Nutsy scrambled back up the bank, shaking the water from his fur. He felt a bit foolish. "I just wanted that big one, Professor Hoot," he mumbled. "It looked so round and firm."

"Indeed," said the old owl. "But perhaps a moment's pause, a careful survey of the path, would have kept you dry and well-fed. One small acorn, lost to the current, is no great tragedy. But many, gathered carelessly, could mean a hungry winter."

Nutsy twitched his nose. "I won't be hungry, Professor Hoot! I'm going to gather more nuts than any squirrel in this forest has ever gathered before. And I'm going to do it the clever way!"

Professor Hoot blinked slowly. "The clever way, you say? And what manner of cleverness might that be?"

"I'm not going to bury them one by one like all the others," Nutsy explained, puffing out his chest. "That takes far too long. I'm going to find one big, secret place, and put all my nuts there. All of them! Then, when winter comes, I'll have a great big store, all in one easy-to-reach spot!"

"Ah," said Professor Hoot. "A grand strategy, to be sure. But the forest, young Nutsy, has many secrets of its own. And sometimes, its secrets do not align with our clever plans."

Nutsy, however, was too excited to heed the owl's subtle warning. He spent the next few days searching for the perfect storage place. He rejected hollow logs as too obvious, abandoned bird nests as too flimsy, and underground burrows as too damp. Finally, he discovered a fissure in a rock face, a narrow, deep crack that seemed to go right into the heart of the hill. "Perfect!" he squeaked with delight. "No one will ever find them here!"

He began his tireless work, gathering every acorn, every hazelnut, every hickory nut he could find. His cheeks bulged almost constantly as he carried load after load to his secret cache. The pile inside the rock fissure grew steadily, a dark mound of winter sustenance. Nutsy envisioned himself, snug and warm, feasting on his treasure while the snow swirled outside.

"Almost done!" he chirped one blustery afternoon, as he carried his last load. He squeezed into the narrow opening, his tail bristling with satisfaction. He pushed the final handful of nuts onto the top of the pile.

And then, with a low groan, the rock shifted. A small tremor ran through the ground. Nutsy paused, his fur suddenly prickling. A shower of pebbles rained down from the roof of the fissure. The opening, through which he had just entered, began to narrow. A deep crack appeared in the rock just above his head.

"Oh, dear!" Nutsy whimpered. He tried to back out, but the opening was already too small. He pushed forward, but his mountain of nuts blocked his way. He was trapped!

"Professor Hoot!" he shrieked, his voice muffled by the rock. "Help! I'm stuck! My clever plan has trapped me!"

High above, Professor Hoot heard the faint cries. He had seen the shifting rock earlier, a tell-tale sign of a weak spot. He slowly flew down, landing on a branch overlooking the fissure. "So, young Nutsy," he hooted softly. "It seems your cleverness has become a clever cage."

"Please help me!" Nutsy cried, scrambling desperately. "I can't get out! And all my nuts are going to be crushed!"

"Patience, little one," Professor Hoot advised. "Thrashing about will only make the rock shift more. I shall fly to Farmer McGregor's barn. He has a small crowbar. Perhaps that will serve."

Nutsy waited, trembling, as the old owl glided away. The fissure groaned again. He thought of the single acorn lost in the creek. How foolish he had been to think one grand plan was better than many small, careful ones.

When Professor Hoot returned, a surprisingly small crowbar clutched in his talons, Farmer McGregor was with him. The farmer carefully assessed the situation. "Looks like young Nutsy got himself in a tight spot," he murmured. "Too eager by half, aren't you, little fellow?"

With a few gentle but firm prods, Farmer McGregor managed to widen the crack just enough for Nutsy to squeeze free. The squirrel burst out, covered in dust and trembling, but unharmed.

"My nuts!" Nutsy exclaimed, looking back at the now sealed fissure. "They're gone!"

"Indeed," said Professor Hoot. "All in one clever basket, young Nutsy. But perhaps, when you have many small baskets, a few lost do not mean a hungry winter for you and your friends."

Nutsy hung his head. "I understand now, Professor Hoot. Slow and steady, and many hiding places. Never again will I put all my hopes in one spot."

"A valuable lesson, learned the hard way," Farmer McGregor said with a smile. "Now, off you go, little rascal. Still plenty of nuts out there, if you're willing to do the honest work."

Nutsy scurried off, no longer quite so eager, but certainly much wiser. He even managed a polite nod to Professor Hoot before he set about searching for new, safe, individual spots for his winter store.

He watched as the blacksmith, a burly man with powerful arms and a kindly face, began to work on the white mare.

Mr. Perkins began by carefully examining the mare's hoof, picking out any bits of stone or dirt. Then he took a sharp, curved knife and a pair of long clippers, and began to trim away the excess horn, shaping the hoof with practiced movements. The sound, though still startling, was now familiar, and Twinkleheels found himself watching the sparks fly with a strange sort of awe. The blacksmith hammered the metal, twisting and turning it, until it began to take the precise shape he desired. He would occasionally hold the hot shoe against the mare's trimmed hoof for just a second, a puff of smoke rising with a peculiar, burnt smell, before returning to the anvil for further adjustments.

Twinkleheels felt a little better, but the smell of burning horn was certainly an odd sensation to him. He watched Mr. Perkins finally quench the shoe in the tub of water, which produced that startling hiss he had heard before. The steam rose, momentarily obscuring the blacksmith, before dissipating into the dusty air. Once cooled, the shoe was dark and dull again, but perfectly shaped.

Mr. Perkins picked up the mare's hoof again, and with a small hammer, began to drive the nails through the shoe and into the hoof. Tap, tap, tap. Each nail went in with a soft, dull sound. Twinkleheels winced slightly with each tap, imagining the feeling. But the mare remained entirely still, her ears flicking occasionally, but otherwise showing no sign of discomfort. He watched as the nails, once driven in, emerged from the outer wall of the hoof, where Mr. Perkins carefully bent them over and then clipped off the ends. He saw the flash of the knife, the snip of the clippers, and the old horse didn't even flinch. He observed the blacksmith holding the red-hot shoe against Ebenezer's hoof, the wisp of smoke, and Ebenezer merely sighed contentedly. It was as if he found the whole process rather relaxing.

patch down by the creek,” Farmer Green continued, pointing with a gnarled finger towards the far end of the farm. “The one where we’re going to plant the new potatoes. It’s too soft for the big plow just yet, and not quite big enough to warrant Bright and Broad’s full attention. A lighter harrow, pulled by a nimble pony, would do well there. Twinkleheels, with his new shoes, might be just the one for it. What do you think, Johnnie?”

Johnnie Green’s face lit up. He turned to Twinkleheels, a wide smile spreading across his features. “That’s a grand idea, Father! Twinkleheels has been itching to do some proper work. And he’s so much stronger and surer-footed now, with his new shoes.”

Twinkleheels felt a thrill run through him, from the tip of his ears to the very soles of his newly shod hoofs. He had indeed been itching for proper work. The praise from Johnnie and Farmer Green made his chest swell with pride. He looked down at his gleaming shoes, remembering the journey to the blacksmith’s shop, the clang and hiss, and his initial terror. Now, those same shoes felt like badges of honor, symbols of his growing courage.

Ebenezer, who had been listening from his stall, let out a soft snort of approval. “A good choice, young fellow,” he murmured to Twinkleheels. “A first step into true service. Mind your pace, and keep your attention on the task at hand. The earth has its own language, and you must learn to listen to it through the harrow.”

Twinkleheels nodded eagerly, though he wasn’t entirely sure what “listening to the earth” meant. He only knew he was ready to try. Johnnie quickly finished harnessing Bright and Broad, leading them out of the barn with Farmer Green. The air filled with the creak of the heavy harness and the rhythmic thump of their massive hooves as they headed towards the vast main field.

“Now, Twinkleheels,” Johnnie said, returning with a much lighter harness, “it’s your turn.” He brought out a small, spiked harrow, its iron teeth gleaming faintly. It looked formidable, but not impossible. “We’ll go down to the creek patch. You’ll smooth the soil after the first turning. It’s important work; it breaks up the clods and prepares a soft bed for the potatoes.”

Twinkleheels felt a flutter of apprehension. He had seen the harrow before, pulled by Ebenezer in his younger days, but he had never been the one pulling it. The spiked teeth looked as though they could catch on roots or stones, causing a nasty jerk. But he reminded himself of Ebenezer’s words: courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. And he had his new shoes; they would give him grip.

Johnnie expertly fitted the harness over Twinkleheels’ back, adjusting the straps until they lay comfortably. Twinkleheels shifted, feeling the unfamiliar weight, but it was not burdensome. “There you go, little friend,” Johnnie said, patting his neck. “Ready for your first big job.”

They walked out of the barn and headed towards the creek, the harrow scraping softly behind them on the packed earth of the lane. The morning air was crisp, carrying the scent of damp soil and awakening spring growth. Birds sang in the trees, and a few early bees buzzed around the budding wildflowers.

As they neared the potato patch, Twinkleheels saw that it was indeed smaller than the main fields, perhaps half an acre. The soil had already been turned by a lighter plow, leaving rows of dark, uneven earth, studded with clods and the occasional stone. It looked like a challenging landscape.

“Now, Twinkleheels,” Johnnie explained, “we’ll start at this end. You need to walk in straight lines, back and forth, overlapping each pass slightly. That way, we get all the soil properly smoothed.” He took hold of the handles of the harrow, positioning Twinkleheels at the edge of the patch.

“Gee up!” Johnnie commanded, a little nervous himself but trying to sound confident.

Twinkleheels leaned into the harness, his new shoes digging firmly into the soft earth. The harrow groaned as it began to move, its teeth biting into the soil. A small cloud of dust rose behind him, smelling of fresh earth. He felt the pull on his shoulders, a steady, constant resistance. It was harder work than he had imagined, but also exhilarating. Each step was a deliberate effort, his muscles working in unison.

He concentrated on keeping his gait even, on walking in as straight a line as possible. The harrow bounced and jolted occasionally as its teeth snagged on a stubborn root or skittered over a hidden stone. Each jolt sent a shiver through Twinkleheels, and for a moment, he would falter, his eyes widening. He remembered the feeling of sinking in the snow, the desperate struggle. But then Johnnie’s steady voice would call out, “Easy, boy, easy now,” and Twinkleheels would regain his composure, pushing forward.

He completed the first pass, turning at the end of the patch with Johnnie’s guidance. The ground behind him looked noticeably smoother, the clods broken into finer soil. A sense of accomplishment began to replace his apprehension. He was doing it. He, Twinkleheels, was truly helping Farmer Green.

He began the second pass, then the third, and the fourth
